attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you brainstorm the functions that might be added to set up the 3 levels and multiple waves, throughout the project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the structure of Red Belt Build activities differ from previous belts in IMPACT?

❓ What functions might be used to set up the 3 levels and multiple waves, throughout the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how the structure of Red Belt will differ from prior belts in IMPACT. In Red Belt, multiple Build activities across the level will be used to construct a larger, complex project based on a given theme (instead of multiple, individual projects). The starter code for each successive Build activity will be populated with code from the previous Build activity. At the end of the level, the ninja will have an opportunity to create their own complex project to add to their Red Belt portfolio, using theme-specific concepts applied throughout the Build activities.

💡 If a ninja is unfamiliar with a tower defense style of game, guide them through the basic features. The user will set up towers throughout the game area. Once towers have been placed, the wave will begin where enemies will move across the screen. The towers will send projectiles towards the enemies. The user’s score increases for each enemy destroyed, but decreases if there are enemies that are able to progress through the path at the end of each wave. Each wave gets progressively faster and more challenging as more enemies appear on screen.

💡 Prompt the ninja to brainstorm specific functions that might be needed to set up the 3 levels and multiple waves, throughout the project. Encourage the ninja to write down ideas as pseudocode to think through the sequence and the logic of the tower defense code.
steps.instructions:
This is the second of 4 Build activities where you will create a tower defense project!


Notice that the code from the Build 1 activity has already been added into the JavaScript editor.


In the second Build activity, you will use the existing code from Build 1 to create a tower defense project with 3 levels, each with 10 waves. You’ll also use the Text Sprite and Story extension to begin UI/UX features to the project.


What functions might be used to set up the 3 levels and multiple waves, throughout the project?

steps.hints: ❓Did you create an if / else if conditional with 5 conditions inside the callScene function, with each condition checking for one of the 5 possible sceneNum values, 0 through 4?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the 3 lines of code under // run game be pasted inside the callScene function definition?

❓ What might happen when each scene is called in the tower defense project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has cut the existing code under // run game then pasted inside the condition that checks if sceneNum equals 2 inside the callScene function. Encourage the ninja to test out the code to ensure it still works as expected, when the callScene(2) is called under // run game.

💡 Prompt the ninja to think through what might happen in the other scenes of the tower defense project. The ninja will be adding multiple levels to the project, as well as a title and closing game sequence. Remind the ninja that creating a custom scene function is a great way to organize the code needed throughout the project.
steps.instructions:
Set up the code to create multiple scenes in the project!


Under // game initialization after the variable and array declarations, add a // game functions comment , then create a callScene function with a sceneNum number parameter. Inside the function definition, use a conditional statement with 5 separate conditions that check if sceneNum equals 0 through 4.


Cut and paste the 3 lines of code under // run game to run when sceneNum equals 2. Then, call the callScene function, passing 2 as the argument, under // run game. 


Click ▶ to test that the tilemap, tile covers, and Cursor sprite load as expected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you pass the sceneNum 2, 3, and 4 to the callScene function to check that the Enemy sprite’s starting position is correct for all 3 tilemaps?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How can you find the starting location for the Enemy sprites in each of the 3 level tilemaps?

❓ What code should be added to the callScene function definition and onUpdateInterval loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can access the tilemap coordinates by opening each level’s tilemap asset, then hovering their mouse over the oceanTile that does not have a tilemap wall on it. Encourage the ninja to test out their code by passing the sceneNum 2, 3, and 4 to the callScene function to check that the Enemy sprite’s starting position is correct for all 3 tilemaps.
steps.instructions:
Add 2 additional levels to the project!


Copy the 3 lines of code that run when sceneNum equals 2 into the conditions that check if sceneNum is equal to 3 and 4. Update the tilemap assets to medLevel and hardLevel respectively.


Under // game initialization, declare a global levelNum number variable set to null. Set levelNum to 1 in the easy level, then 2 and 3 in the respective level scenes in the callScene function definition.


The levelNum  variable will be used to set the Enemy sprite starting position. Under // game wave functions and events, find the code inside the onUpdateInterval loop that creates the Enemy sprite. Add a blank line underneath, then create a nested conditional that checks for the 3 possible levelNum values. Cut and paste the placeOnTile function to set the different starting point for the Enemy sprites in each of the 3 tilemaps. Open the tilemap asset for their respective levels to see the coordinates of the starting tile.


Under // run game, test out each level by updating the callScene function call argument to check that the Enemy sprites start in the correct spot for all 3 scenes. Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprites appear on screen and begin to walk across the different paths.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a tileAtLocationEquals function to check for the rightArrow, downArrow, and leftRightArrow assets in each conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which tilemap function should be used to check if a tile at a certain location is equal to a specific image?

❓ What code should be passed as the location parameter in the tileAtLocationEquals function to access the Enemy sprite’s tilemap location?

❓ What should the Enemy sprite’s x- and y-velocity be set to when it overlaps each of the possible arrow tiles?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use the tileAtLocationEquals function to check if the wall tile at the Enemy sprite’s location is equal to each arrow tile image.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the sprite variable, not the location variable, from the onHitWall function to check the sprite's location compared to the tile it is overlapping. The location parameter in each tileAtLocationEquals function should look like: 

sprite.tilemapLocation()

💡 Prompt the ninja to open My Assets to identify the names of each arrow tile to use in the code.
steps.instructions:
Code the Enemy sprites to follow the arrows on the path!


Under // game functions, below the callScene function definition, use an onHitWall function to change an Enemy sprite’s velocity when it hits a tilemap wall. Inside, use an if/else if/else if conditional that checks if the tile at the wall location equals each of the 3 possible arrow tiles on the medLevel and hardLevel tilemaps. Use the onHitWall’s sprite variable, a dot operator, and tilemapLocation() to find the tilemap location of an Enemy sprite in the tileAtLocationEquals function that is part of each condition. 


Inside each condition, update the Enemy sprite’s velocity so that it moves in the direction of the arrow tile. For the arrow tile that points both left and right, use a nested conditional that uses a percent chance to set the sprite velocity to move either left or right.


Click ▶ to test the Enemy sprite movement when it overlaps the arrow tiles in the medium and hard levels. Do not place any Tower sprites during testing so that the Enemy sprite movement can be observed!

steps.hints: ❓Did you cover each arrow tile with a sand tile that matches the direction the arrow tile is pointing in?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Does each Enemy sprite’s movement work as expected on the medium and hard level tilemaps?

❓ Which tiles should cover each arrow tile code in the coverAllTiles functions?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to open the medium and hard level tilemaps in My Assets, then explore the path tile options in My Tiles to update the code with tiles that should cover each arrow.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the movement of the Enemy sprites. Prompt them to consider why the coverAllTiles function does not affect the sprites’ interactions with the tiles being covered.
steps.instructions:
Cover the arrow tiles with path tiles.


Under // game functions, in the coverTiles function definition, add 3 additional coverAllTiles functions to cover each arrow tile kind with one of the path tile options found in My Assets. 


The coverAllTiles function will change the appearance of a tile, but will not change how a sprite reacts to the original tile “under” the cover. 


Call sceneNum 3 and 4 then click ▶ to test that the tiles are covered correctly, and that the Enemy sprites still change direction when overlapping those tiles, as expected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you create a conditional that uses 10 separate conditions to check for wave numbers 1-10?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the startWave function is called, if waveNum equals 1 or 2?

❓ What might happen differently in each of the 10 waves?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use Ctrl + F to search for function names in the code to access them easily.

💡 When the startWave function is called and waveNum equals 1, 4 red crab images will spawn and move across the path tiles. If waveNum equals 2, 8 red crab images will spawn and move across the path tiles.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider how the updated number argument in each spawnEnemy function call differs from the waveNum * 3 code that was there previously. In each wave, the number of Enemy sprites spawned will continue to increase, however in the next step, crabs of different colors will be added in each wave (which is why it doesn’t make sense to just multiply the waveNum by 3 anymore).
steps.instructions:
Spawn a different number of Enemy sprites in each wave!


Under // game wave functions and events, in the startWave function definition, replace the spawnEnemy function call with a conditional that uses 10 different conditions to check if waveNum is equal to 1 through 10. In a later step, display text will be added to let users know which wave they are playing.


If  waveNum equals 1, call the spawnEnemy function, passing the redCrabImage and the number 4 as arguments. This will add 4 red crab images to the enemyImages array, which will then be used to create Enemy sprites in the onUpdateInterval loop. 


When it equals 2, call the spawnEnemy function again with the same image but the number 8 as arguments.

steps.hints: ❓Did you create 10 different waves of Enemy sprites, making each one harder than the last?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How many Enemy sprites might be spawned in each wave?

❓ How might you sequence the code so that different colored Enemy sprites appear in different orders in each wave?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the ninja wants to test out the code, encourage them to comment out the line of code in the onUpdateInterval loop that animates the crab. This will allow the ninja to see the "still" images change color and move on screen. Otherwise, this will be addressed in the next step.

💡 Encourage the ninja to think through the sequence of the spawnEnemy functions and the arguments passed to each function. Remind the ninja that blue and green colored Enemy sprites will require more power to defeat, and they should add them to each wave strategically.
steps.instructions:
Spawn different colors of Enemy sprites that are more difficult to destroy!


If  waveNum equals 3, call the spawnEnemy function 2 times, passing the redCrabImage and 3 in the first call, and blueCrabImage and 3 in the second call. This will add 3 red crab images and 3 blue crab images to the enemyImages array. Continue adding various numbers and combinations of red and blue crabs for waves 4 through 7.


If  waveNum equals 8, 9, or 10, call the spawnEnemy function using either the redCrabImage, the blueCrabImage, or the greenCrabImage. 


Keep in mind, each wave should be more challenging than the previous level, and the different colored Enemy sprites will take longer to defeat!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the enemySprite.image.equals() function to check for the color of each Enemy sprite in the conditional statements?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What function should be used to check if a sprite’s image matches a specific image asset?

❓ Which spawnEnemy functions might be updated so that each wave is progressively harder than the previous one?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to use the enemySprite.image.equals() function inside each conditional to check for the Enemy sprite’s image. Remind the ninja that the enemySprite variable is initialized at the beginning of the project, so it can be accessed inside of any function throughout the project’s code.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the different waves of the project. Prompt them to consider which waves have the expected number of each colored Enemy sprite and which might be updated to make the wave more or less challenging.
steps.instructions:
Animate the different colored Enemy sprites!


In the onUpdateInterval loop, add a conditional after the code that sets the Enemy sprite’s starting location. Use the conditional to check for the 3 different Enemy sprite colors, then update the Enemy sprite’s animation asset to match the color of the sprite.


In the endWave function definition, add a conditional that will end the game in a win if gameWaveCount equals 10 when the function is called. Cut and paste the rest of the code into an else condition.


Click ▶ to test the waves of different colored Enemy sprites, then adjust the spawnEnemy functions and their parameters to refine the quantity of Enemy sprites and the challenge of each Enemy sprite wave.

steps.hints: ❓Did you check for the Enemy sprite color in the conditional in this order: red, then blue, then green? If not, the overlap code may not consistently work as expected.
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Do the Enemy sprites change colors as expected when each wave is tested?

❓ Which colored Enemy sprite is hardest to destroy? Why?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 It’s important that the overlap code addresses the red, then blue, then green crab in that order. When reversed, the overlap can continue to be triggered as the color changes, and the desired result will not be achieved.

💡 Now, green Enemy sprites will need to be hit by a projectile three times, blue Enemy sprites twice, and red Enemy sprites once, in order to be destroyed.
steps.instructions:
Change the Enemy sprite color when overlapped by a Projectile to make them harder to destroy!


Under // game play events, inside the Projectile/Enemy overlap code, add a conditional that checks if the Enemy sprite is red, blue, then green. Cut the existing destroy code and paste it into the condition for the redCrabImage. 


For the blueCrabImage, destroy the Projectile sprite, but change the Enemy sprite image and animation to that of the red crab. This will change the blue Enemy to a red Enemy, extending its life.


For the greenCrabImage, destroy the Projectile sprite, but change the Enemy sprite image and animation to that of the blue crab. This will change the green Enemy to a blue Enemy, which extends its life even more!


Click ▶ to test the challenge level of the different colored Enemy sprites!

steps.hints: ❓Did you define the createTextSprite function’s parameters in the order they are used inside the function definition to make it easier to use them?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the createTextSprite function be used for in the tower defense project?

❓ Why might it be useful to define a custom function with several parameters (7)?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Custom functions can be very useful in large, complex projects. By creating a function with several parameters, the ninja can reuse the function many times throughout the project. Parameters help customize the code that runs inside the function; this will allow the ninja to easily create text sprites of different messages, sizes, colors, icons, etc. at multiple points in the project.

💡 Remind the ninja that when adding the 7 parameters to their createTextSprite function, different data types require lowercase and capital letters. Images and Sprite parameters should be capitalized, and numbers and strings should be lowercase. The code might look like:

(text: string, fgColor: number, icon: Image, sprite: Sprite)
steps.instructions:
Create a function that will display text on screen to track lives and money.


First, add the arcade-text extension to the project. 


Add a ScreenText sprite kind. Then, under // sprite initialization, declare a textSprite TextSprite variable set to null. 


Under // game functions, define a createTextSprite function with 7 parameters: a string parameter (text), 5 number parameters (fgColor, bgColor, fontSize, xPos, yPos) and an image parameter (icon). 


Inside the function definition, use textsprite.create to create a text sprite using the text, bgColor, and fgColor function parameters. Set the font size and position using the other number parameters. Set the text sprite’s icon using the image parameter. Last, set the text sprite’s sprite kind to ScreenText.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use convertToText to convert the lives number variable to a string?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where does the lives variable appear on screen? 

❓ Does it appear as expected? What might be adjusted?

❓ What function is needed to convert a number value into a string that can be passed to a text sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninjas that text sprite font sizes can be set to multiples of 5 or 8 (which represent 2 different font types). 

💡 Remind the ninja to use the convertToText function to convert the lives number variable to a string that can be displayed on screen.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the project repeatedly, then update the arguments passed to the createTextSprite function to change the ScreenText sprite’s appearance and position on screen.
steps.instructions:
Add a lives variable and display the user’s lives on screen!


Under // game initialization, declare a lives number variable set to null. Then, set lives to 20 inside the initializeLevel function definition.


Under // game functions, define a createScreenText function. Inside, call the createTextSprite function, passing arguments that will set the lives variable to display next to the playTile, using colors that stand out against the tilemap and the livesIcon image asset. 


Above the createTextSprite function call, destroy all of the existing ScreenText sprites to remove any on-screen text before creating new ScreenText sprites.


Call the createScreenText function inside the initializeLevel function definition.


Click ▶ test the colors and placement of the lives ScreenText sprite.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the sprite.image.equals() function to check for the color of each Enemy sprite in the conditional statements?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where can code be copied from and pasted inside the onOverlapTile function for efficiency?

❓ What symbols should be used to update the value of the the lives variable?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to copy (Ctrl + C) and paste (Ctrl + V) from elsewhere in the project into the onOverlapTile function for efficiency. They already have code that checks for the 3 different Enemy sprite image assets, which can then be copied and pasted into the onOverlapTile function. Remind the ninja to delete any code that doesn’t need to be copied as well.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use – to decrease a variable by 1, and a subtraction assignment operator -= to decrease then reassign a variable’s value.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the lives variable code to ensure it updates correctly when Enemy sprites overlap the endTile. Prompt the ninja to tinker with the number and colors of Enemy sprites in each wave, if the lives variable is decreasing too quickly. 

💡 Creating their own lives variable, instead of using the default MakeCode one, allows the ninja to customize how the variable is updated and displayed on screen.
steps.instructions:
Change the lives variable when Enemy sprites overlap the end tile.﻿


Inside the onOverlapTile function for the Enemy sprite and the endTile, add a conditional that checks for the 3 different Enemy sprite image assets, then destroys the Enemy sprite inside each condition.


Then, decrease the lives variable by 1 for the redCrabImage, 2 for the blueCrabImage, and 3 for the greenCrabImage. Call the createScreenText function after the conditional to update the lives variable on screen.


Add another conditional inside the event that ends the game in a loss if lives is less than or equal to 0.


Click ▶ to see the lives variable display change as the Enemy sprites reach the end of the path.

steps.hints: ❓Did you call the createScreenText function inside both the initializeLevel function definition and the Projectile/Enemy onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you copy the existing createTextSprite function call inside the createScreenText function definition, then update the arguments to display the money variable on screen?

❓ How much money is earned for every Enemy sprite destroyed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 An economy system within a game provides players with another layer of strategy in which they have to be mindful of how many towers they have and where they should be placed. Limiting the amount of towers will improve the user experience and make the game more engaging.

💡 Encourage the ninja to copy (Ctrl + C) and paste (Ctrl + V) to duplicate the existing createTextSprite function call inside the createScreenText function definition. Prompt the ninja to tinker with the arguments so that the money variable is displayed with a different color and icon image, in the top left corner of the screen.

💡 Prompt the ninja to test out the project to ensure that the money variable increases by 10, each time an Enemy sprite is destroyed. Encourage the ninja to tinker with the number of Enemy sprites in each wave and/or the appearance of the money variable to customize the code.
steps.instructions:
Create an internal economy system that lets users earn money when they destroy an enemy! Add a money variable and display the money earned by destroying Enemy sprites on screen.


Under // game initialization, declare a money number variable set to null. Then, inside the initializeLevel function definition, set money to 200 before the createScreenText function call.


Inside the createScreenText function, call the createTextSprite function, passing arguments that will set the money variable to display in the upper left corner of the screen, using colors that stand out against the tilemap and the moneyIcon image asset.


Inside the Projectile/Enemy overlap code, increase money by 10 in all 3 conditions. Then call the createScreenText function after the conditional to update the money variable on screen.


Click ▶ then place multiple Tower sprites on the tilemap and start the game wave to see the money variable increase as Enemy sprites are destroyed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use && to check that the Cursor sprite is above a sandTile and the money variable is greater than or equal to 100 before a new Tower sprite is created?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How much does a Tower sprite cost to place? How does this change the game?

❓ What conditions need to be true in order to place a Tower sprite on the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the user presses the A button, a Tower sprite can be created if the Cursor sprite is above a sandTile and the money variable is greater than or equal to 100. The money variable will decrease by 100 once a Tower sprite is created.

💡 In the next Build activity, the ninja will add additional Tower sprites of different sizes which will cost different amounts to purchase and place.
steps.instructions:
Allow users to spend money to build more defense towers by changing the money variable when a Tower sprite is created.


Inside the conditional that’s inside the A button pressed event, reduce the money variable by 100 above the code that creates a new Tower sprite. Then call the createScreenText function underneath to update the money variable on screen.


Inside the condition that checks for the sandTile tile asset, use an AND operator to also check that the money variable is greater than or equal to 100 to ensure there is enough money available to purchase a Tower sprite.


Click ▶ to see the money variable decrease as Tower sprites are placed on the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the code documentation box to fill in each of the createTextSprite function arguments and pass a font size parameter that is a multiple of 5 or 8 to create a larger text sprite on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might the game wave text sprite be placed on screen when the wave begins?

❓ Does the text sprite appear as expected? What values might be adjusted?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use the code documentation box to fill in each of the createTextSprite function arguments. The game wave text sprite does not need to appear on the same top line as the money variable, lives variable, and endTile.
steps.instructions:
Display the game wave number on screen before it starts.


Inside the startWave function definition, call the createTextSprite function above the other code already inside the definition. Use the string “Wave “ plus the waveNum parameter to display the game wave number in a large font in the center of the screen. Pass null as the icon parameter, since an image is not needed for this text sprite.


Use the textSprite variable to set the lifespan of the game wave text sprite so it disappears after 1.5 to 2 seconds.


Click ▶ to see the game wave number appear on screen at the start of each new game wave.

steps.hints: ❓Did you pass null as the icon parameter for the text sprites in this step, since no image is needed for them?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the title of the tower defense project be?

❓ What colors might be used on the title screen to make the text pop on screen?

❓ What scene should be called to test the title screen code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to pass 0 to the callScene function to ensure the title screen appears on screen. Encourage the ninja to test the title screen multiple times, then adjust the argument values in the createTextSprite function calls to modify the title’s appearance.

💡 This code will act as a placeholder to complete the structure of a complete project. More extensive UI/UX features will be added in Build 3 to create a more interactive and detailed user experience.
steps.instructions:
Create a splash screen for the project!


Inside the callScene function definition, when the sceneNum parameter equals 0, add a // splash screen comment, then set a background color and use the createTextSprite function to display the title of the game on the upper middle part of the screen.


Under // run game, change the parameter passed to the callScene function to 0 so the game title displays on screen.


Click ▶ to see the game title appear on screen, then adjust the font size, style, and color until it appears correctly.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add callScene(1) to the end of the code that runs when sceneNum equals 0?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might the level select text be placed on screen?

❓ What level choices might the user be given at the beginning of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to copy/paste or type the string text exactly in the checkLastAnswer functions as it appears in the showPlayerChoices function.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the level select menu and adjust the argument values passed to the createTextSprite function as needed. Prompt the ninja to test the sequence of the callScene function to ensure the correct level is called, based on the user’s choice.

💡 This code will act as a placeholder to complete the structure of a complete project. More extensive UI/UX features will be added in Build 3 to create a more interactive and detailed user experience.
steps.instructions:
Create a level select menu to choose from the 3 different level options!


Inside the callScene function definition, inside the condition when sceneNum equals 1, add a // level select menu comment, then call the createTextSprite function to ask the player to select a level from the menu that will appear below it.


Add the arcade-story extension to the project. 


Then, use the showPlayerChoices function to offer the player a menu of 3 levels of difficulty. Create a  conditional (nested inside the condition when sceneNum equals 1) with 3 checkLastAnswer functions for each level of difficulty. Inside each condition, use the callScene function to call sceneNum 2, 3, or 4 based on the level of difficulty selected.


Inside the callScene function definition, when the sceneNum parameter equals 0, call the callScene function with the argument 1 so the level select menu shows below the game title.


Click ▶ to see the level select menu, then adjust the position and size of the text sprites until everything fits on screen correctly.

subgroups.introduction: Continue building a Tower Defense project that includes different Enemy types and multiple paths. Expand to multiple levels and enemy types, create a game economy that allows users to earn and spend money, and add UI/UX features to the project so the user gets feedback on their game experience.

validationItems.text: Create a callScene function with a number parameter. Use the number parameter to call scenes numbered 0-4.

Set the different tilemaps that will appear when the callScene function is called with different arguments. Create a levelNum variable that is used to set the Enemy sprites’ starting position on each tilemap.
Code the Enemy sprites to follow the tilemap path. Cover the arrow tiles on the path.
Create 10 different waves of animated Enemy sprites. Change the Enemy sprite’s color when overlapped by a Projectile.
Create a function that can be used to display on-screen text.
Create lives and money variables, then display both variables on screen.
Change the lives variable when Enemy sprites overlap the end tile. Change the money variable when Tower sprites are created or Enemy sprites are destroyed. Display the updated variables on screen.
Use text sprites to display text on the level select screen and as the game wave begins.

requirements.functionName: createTextSprite(text, fgColor, bgColor, fontSize, xPos, yPos, icon)

validationItems.text: Create a level select menu that will call the appropriate tilemap based on the user’s choice.
